Was it this case? The one that made you lose faith in the justice system?
Forensica's expression shifts in an instant.
She stares at the file as though it were something vile.
The crime scene where you stole the corpse from was staged exactly like the Origami Killer's previous cases.
Back then, you suspected a case to be the work of them, but you couldn't get authorization from your institution or the victim's family. You tried to perform an unauthorized autopsy and got caught.
From that day forward, you were branded a problematic forensic pathologist and got blacklisted from ever practicing officially again.

speaker: Forensica
content: How do you have this...?
Forensica asks in a low voice, and you can hear her teeth grinding.

speaker: Forensica
content: And? Are you pitying me? Mocking me? Or are you planning to use this against me?

options: I want to understand the truth.

speaker: Forensica
content: Help me? What, are you going to use your privileges as MBCC Chief and lead a bunch of freak Sinners on a rampage to hunt down the killer or something?

speaker: Forensica
content: Hahaha, don't make me laugh. What do you even know? All you people do is make empty promises.

speaker: Forensica
content: The truth... Yeah, if it weren't for the truth, I wouldn't have ended up like this either.

speaker: Forensica
content: And why should I give you the truth just because you asked? I didn't see anyone giving me the truth when I wanted it!
I understand that I can't earn your trust overnight.
But as a forensic pathologist who is able to draw conclusions based on objective facts and scientific evidence, you should have grounds to believe me.

speaker: Forensica
content: And what would that be? Your superpowers?
We both played a role in solving the orphanage arson case, and our work was recognized by the renowned author Clementine. I believe that demonstrates my ability to uncover the truth.

speaker: Forensica
content: ...I suppose you're right.
And secondly, there's this.

options: Autopsy consent form and morgue key

speaker: Forensica
content: This is...
A postmortem examination requested under the Bureau's authority. Mania infection may cause unusual changes in corpses that require further autopsy to confirm.
It's all by the book.
I'm certain you need these. You don't have to trust me, but you can feel free to use me. Use my position, and my authority.
Isn't it your wish to find the evidence and truth you're looking for through autopsy?
Forensica falls silent for a long time. She lowers her head to look at her hands, her fingers tracing the outline of the bone in her pocket.
She murmurs, though it's unclear who she's speaking to.

speaker: Forensica
content: Why? Why would you go this far...

speaker: Forensica
content: What do you want from me? I have nothing I can give you...

speaker: Forensica
content: The truth... Is there someone in this world who actually cares about the truth?

speaker: Forensica
content: Sometimes, even I wonder... does truth really exist? And even if I do find it, what difference does it make?
Forensica stares at the files of the Origami Killer. She's been trapped in this case for far too long.

Because of this case, she was blacklisted from the industry, spent her days holed up in a basement, cut off contact with her parents to avoid dragging anyone else down, was hunted by forces in the shadows, and even wandered into a contamination zone, becoming a Sinner.
Because of this case, her life was torn apart.
Forensica has often felt that she's not just fighting the killer. The massive power structure, as monstrous as any beast, is also standing against her.

speaker: Forensica
content: Why are you doing all this?

speaker: Forensica
content: It'd be much easier for you to just follow protocol—put me on trial, convict me, and lock me away.

speaker: Forensica
content: Disturbing public safety and desecrating corpses... these are trivial charges, really.

speaker: Forensica
content: Especially when you consider how terrible my record is already.
What I want isn't submission. It's the truth.
If you're willing to complete the autopsy under my supervision, you can continue using me.
I believe I've shown you enough to prove that my value to you is extremely high. Am I wrong?
The confusion in Forensica's eyes gradually gives way to resolve. She takes a deep breath. It seems that she's made a decision.

speaker: Forensica
content: Fine. I'll accept your offer.
Tomorrow morning, nine o'clock. I'll see you at the morgue.
You rise to leave, but Forensica's voice stops you.

speaker: Forensica
content: In the novel... did I really give you the finger bone?
Yes. You said it was your good luck charm.
Take us away! You should get us out of here!
Forensica doesn't speak another word. The corners of her mouth subtly curl up, barely visible.
She extends her pinky and hooks it around the finger bone jutting from her pocket, her eyes brimming with anticipation for tomorrow's autopsy.
Cold white light illuminates every tile of the floor evenly. The air is thick with the scent of formalin and disinfectant.
An autopsy table made of stainless steel stands at the center of the room, draped in a white shroud.
Forensica is already there, fully suited in protective gear, meticulously inspecting her autopsy tools.
The gleaming dissection instruments are laid out neatly on the surgical tray, cold and sharp.
Hope I'm not late.

speaker: Forensica
content: As the supervisor, I'd say... you barely made it on time.
Forensica looks far more composed and professional than yesterday. Her eyes are calm and focused.
You suit up in protective gear and a mask. The way you put on sterile gloves with practiced ease catches Forensica's attention.
I'm more than just a supervisor today. I'll also be your assistant.

speaker: Forensica
content: Heh, to think I'll have the great MBCC Chief as my assistant. I bet most people would be trembling with excitement at such an honor.

speaker: Forensica
content: But you should know I'm not like most people. I'll call you out regardless if you mess up.
Forensica pulls away the shroud, revealing the body of a middle-aged man. You notice prominent wounds on his wrists.
She calmly proceeds with the autopsy, technical terminology coming out one after another from behind her mask.

speaker: Forensica
content: The deceased is a middle-aged male, approximately 175 centimeters in height, 70 kilograms in weight.

speaker: Forensica
content: Horizontal wound observed on the wrist, approximately 1.2 centimeters in depth. Wound margins are clean, with minimal scabbing present.
Looks like suicide.

speaker: Forensica
content: Congratulations on reaching the same conclusion as all those other idiots.
...I'm just stating what the evidence shows.

speaker: Forensica
content: Yes, suicide. Simple and convenient. Who needs thorough investigations or questions when you can just chalk everything up to suicide, right?

speaker: Forensica
content: Use your eyes. It's obviously not that.

speaker: Forensica
content: Don't take it the wrong way. I'm not mocking you specifically. Most people are blind during an autopsy.
Forensica meticulously examines the wounds and skin, repeatedly verifying details as she voices her findings.
It's almost as if there's no need for any hypotheses when she's here—a single glance is all she needs to reach the most accurate conclusion.

speaker: Forensica
content: Wound margins show slight retraction from post-mortem desiccation. There are no patterns typical of arterial spray or deep clotting from vascular rupture.

speaker: Forensica
content: Meaning that the wrists were cut while the victim was dying or already dead. It's only staged to look like suicide.
Forensica lightly palpates the neck, finding exactly what she was looking for.
She raises her hand, gesturing for you to pick up the scalpel with forceps and place the handle in her palm.
Forensica makes an incision along the neck, her movements precise and efficient, just like a surgeon performing an operation.

speaker: Forensica
content: Slight swelling above the thyroid cartilage. Petechial hemorrhaging visible beneath the skin.

speaker: Forensica
content: Oral mucosa intact, though slight abrasions can be found in the posterior pharyngeal wall.

speaker: Forensica
content: Facial cyanosis and ruptured capillaries in the nail beds. Consistent with asphyxiation.

speaker: Forensica
content: Suicide after excessive drinking due to depression? Yeah right—

speaker: Forensica
content: This is the Origami Killer's signature methodology. Using massive blood loss to mask the real cause of death—asphyxiation.
But if there's all this evidence available... why would they conclude that it's suicide and close the case just like that?

speaker: Forensica
content: What else? Career advancement, good optics, maintaining the illusion of peace and order...

speaker: Forensica
content: Serial killings cause public panic. Suicide, on the other hand, would never cause a ruckus, especially when the victim isn't anyone important. There's no need for them to dig any deeper than that.

speaker: Forensica
content: And the public only sees what those in power want them to see.

speaker: Forensica
content: As for the truth? It'll just be buried along with these bodies. No one cares anyway.
You open your mouth to say something, but ultimately decide against it.
Forensica isn't making baseless claims—what she describes happens all too often in reality. But your own experiences tell you that not everyone is like that.
You just hope she'll be able to believe in someone or something again, even if just a little.
According to the case files, the Origami Killer usually leaves origami flowers at the crime scene, but there doesn't seem to be any near this body.

speaker: Forensica
content: That's because they know I'm just a step away from finding them.

speaker: Forensica
content: I might not know who this bastard is right now, but one thing's for sure—I've been inching closer to the truth over the years.

speaker: Forensica
content: At first, the origami flowers were like a signature, a way for the killer to show off. They'd appear around the bodies.

speaker: Forensica
content: People knew the Origami Killer existed, but had no idea how they killed.

speaker: Forensica
content: Suicide, homicide, accident, allergic reaction... When it comes to how the victims found near the origami flowers died, there were no patterns to speak of.

speaker: Forensica
content: But I knew better. I knew that it was all a cover-up and that they actually all died of asphyxiation.

speaker: Forensica
content: With enough samples, it was only a matter of time before I found the killer.

speaker: Forensica
content: And so, they stopped leaving behind origami flowers, hoping the bodies would blend in with routine deaths so that they could avoid getting exposed.

speaker: Forensica
content: But what hasn't changed is their method of killing. The killer is intelligent and cautious, but they're also arrogant and proud.
There are many ways to cause asphyxiation... And we can't eliminate the possibility of someone copying the method of killing either.

speaker: Forensica
content: ...You're quite interesting.

speaker: Forensica
content: I thought you'd be just another pretentious idiot, but it turns out you actually can get things done. You're quite sharp too.

speaker: Forensica
content: That wasn't a compliment. Smart people have it rough.

speaker: Forensica
content: The world's been taken over by idiots, and smart people are forced to play by their rules because of that.

speaker: Forensica
content: You've got a long way to go if you actually want to earn my recognition.

speaker: Forensica
content: Well, you're already better than most people I've met though. Corpses included.
So, the key evidence is in the asphyxiation wounds?

speaker: Forensica
content: I extracted some fiber fragments from one of the victims' throats before.

speaker: Forensica
content: The killer would crumple a special type of paper into a ball before forcing it down the victim's throat, suffocating them.

speaker: Forensica
content: There's a significant amount of fibrin deposits around the hemorrhage sites, and the pattern matches the marks left by paper balls.
Forensica pulls a small glass vial from her pocket. Inside are dark brown scraps.
She holds the vial up to a shadowless lamp. Her pupils widen, eyes ablaze with fierce intensity.

speaker: Forensica
content: These are paper scraps I collected from one of the victims' throats.

speaker: Forensica
content: They were likely left behind when the killer removed the paper ball.

speaker: Forensica
content: After that, the killer grew more and more skilled, and left fewer and fewer traces behind.

speaker: Forensica
content: If I can extract fiber fragments of the same material from this corpse's throat, that would prove the Origami Killer's the one who did it.
You piece together the years-long battle between Forensica and this Origami Killer—two adversaries who have never met.
The Origami Killer would leave folded paper at each crime scene. It's a signature, a mark symbolizing another victory.
Forensica uncovered the victims' true cause of death, deciphered the killer's method, and recovered paper fragments as evidence.
The Origami Killer caught on. They grew more cautious, and more restrained. In subsequent cases, they stopped leaving origami flowers behind.
The killer might be extremely arrogant, but they're also intelligent and composed. They haven't lost control of themselves even once.
Without the origami flowers, no one but Forensica can trace the cases back to them.

speaker: Forensica
content: I swear I'll catch this bastard!
You seem particularly invested in this killer. Is there another reason why?
Forensica falls silent for a moment. She doesn't answer the question, and instead continues with the autopsy.
You assist by passing her tools and recording data. The two of you work together remarkably well, as if you've done this many times before.
Forensica extracts some more samples from several key areas and runs further tests.
She watches you record the data, and suddenly speaks.

speaker: Forensica
content: Your hands are very steady. Nothing like those clumsy assistants I've had.
I've had some training before.
You flip through the recorded data. Just then, the edge of the paper cuts your finger.
The blood doesn't spread. You recall that when you were writing earlier, the paper seemed harder to write on than regular paper.
This paper is such a pain to use. Since we have to write without anything underneath it half the time, can't we use something easier to write on?

speaker: Forensica
content: What would you know? This paper is rigid enough and doesn't get stained by liquids easily. Not to mention, it's fire-resistant and easy to preserve.

speaker: Forensica
content: I've been using it ever since I was a student...
Forensica suddenly freezes in place. She seems to have realized something, her chest pounding.
She rushes to the lab bench and reaches for the glass vial containing the paper sample with trembling hands.
She then lifts the fiber sample from the vial using tweezers, and holds it over the flame of an alcohol lamp.
What are you doing? That's key evidence, isn't it?
Forensica stares at the fiber burning in the flame, eyes wide, breathing rapidly.
The fiber doesn't burn completely. Instead, a small fragment remains, even after being exposed to the fire.
Forensica's hand goes slack. The tweezers drop to the floor and clatter. She stumbles back, her face ghastly pale.
What did you find?

speaker: Forensica
content: How did I overlook something so simple...?
The shackles in your consciousness jolt suddenly. Forensica turns around and bolts to the door. She doesn't even remove her surgical gown or gloves, and simply rushes out of the morgue.
Her speed is staggering, and with her special power allowing for brief invisibility, she vanishes at the end of the corridor in an instant.
The next day, Chief's Office
Forensica vanished without a trace after yesterday. The burned sample sits on your desk.

She must have discovered something. That's why she reacted so strongly. You mobilized a search party overnight to track her down, but it wasn't until the following morning that you received news from Nightingale.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Chief, the higher-ups have issued their report on Forensica's case and their ruling.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Forensica attempted to break into the DisCity University's School of Forensic Science last night. She was apprehended by security.

speaker: Nightingale
content: She's currently being held on charges of disturbing the peace and unauthorized handling of potentially infectious remains.
At least we know where she is. Can you arrange for her to be transferred into our custody? Given her current state, she could easily lose control.

speaker: Nightingale
content: I've already negotiated with them. They say she's emotionally stable at the moment, but she refuses to answer any questions. And since she escaped from MBCC custody, they're reluctant to send her back to us.
Nightingale shakes her head, then pulls out an evidence bag from her folder and hands it to you.

speaker: Nightingale
content: However, I was able to secure a visit with her. She asked me to pass this along to you.
You take the evidence bag. Inside is a scrap of paper torn from a forensic record sheet. The words "School of Forensic Science" and a name are written on it.
Aster... Wynne?
Do you know anything about this person?

speaker: Nightingale
content: I had someone look into her as soon as I received the note. According to our records, she's an outstanding graduate of the School of Forensic Science and happens to be Forensica's senior. She's a forensic pathologist with an eccentric personality, but her talent is undeniable.

speaker: Nightingale
content: After graduation, she was expelled from both the School of Forensic Science and the Forensic Association for "misconduct."
Sounds awfully similar to Forensica.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Indeed. She appears to be another eccentric genius.
What was the reason for her expulsion?

speaker: Nightingale
content: According to the Association's official statement, she "lacks reverence for life" and "places her own will above all else."
Those are pretty serious charges...

speaker: Nightingale
content: I interviewed several people connected to her, including former mentors and colleagues. They said she frequently altered autopsy procedures without authorization and even took tissue samples without permission to conduct experiments.

speaker: Nightingale
content: She was also once authorized to conduct tests on critically ill or dying patients for data.

speaker: Nightingale
content: But as her demands grew increasingly bizarre and cruel, she was ultimately expelled and blacklisted. The Association never disclosed the specifics of what she did either.
I take that back. Forensica is far better than her.

speaker: Nightingale
content: After her expulsion, Aster vanished for a time before reappearing in the residential areas on the outskirts of Eastside.
Nightingale hands you another stack of documents and points to a particular section.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Shortly after that, the first Origami Killer case occurred.

The documents show that Aster, the expelled forensic pathologist, was once listed as a suspect in the Origami Killer cases. However, everyone who lived near her testified that she was just a shut-in who kept to herself, and they never noticed anything unusual about her.
As you flip through the pages, you notice that critical evidence, such as alibis and the like, is completely absent. She was cleared of suspicion based solely on a few flimsy testimonies.
You stare at the news article. If Forensica wanted to convey a message to you, it must be related to the culprit.
The burned paper fibers on the desk remind you of Forensica's words in the morgue.

Forensic recording paper is rigid and doesn't get easily stained by liquids. If someone crumples something like that into a ball and forces it down a person's throat, it'd make for the perfect murder weapon.
And if the killer is a forensic pathologist, she would know exactly how to forge wounds, conceal evidence... and choose her victims.
The case that led to Forensica's expulsion involved a victim named Eligy. The origami flower pattern at the scene matched those found in the Origami Killer cases.
Forensica discovered discrepancies and demanded further autopsy, but the victim's family suddenly withdrew their complaint and prepared for immediate burial.
In search for evidence, Forensica forcibly performed the autopsy, but was interrupted by the director and the victim's family. The incident was deemed a serious violation and led to her expulsion.
Even so, Forensica didn't give up. She set her sights on the Origami Killer and tried anything she could to uncover cases connected to the culprit.
Those stripped of their status become decadent, depraved, fading into obscurity.
It's something that has happened to Aster and Forensica alike, yet they walked completely different paths.
No one suspected that she would murder anyone, and no one noticed when she did either. Or perhaps... they did suspect something, but weren't allowed to voice it.
When power escapes the scrutiny of the public, those who hold it quickly become narrow-minded and arrogant.
Yet, such is life. It is a paradoxical thing that can bring hope and destruction all the same.
It's just like this forensic record sheet. It can be evidence that reveals the truth, or a weapon that enables murder.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Chief, what do we do now?
Now that we know the truth, I intend to keep my promise. I will give Forensica the justice she seeks.
Both procedural and moral justice.
The courtroom is solemn and imposing. Everyone lowers their face instinctively in the face of the dark seats and cavernous dome.
The gallery is packed. There are jury members, reporters, and professors from the School of Forensic Science here. Even the families of the victims are present.
This isn't your first time attending a trial, but it is the first time you're appearing as both plaintiff and witness.
To expedite evidence collection and fast-track the trial proceedings, you pulled some strings as the MBCC Chief.
It isn't exactly by the book, but just as Forensica said—rules bend for those in power.

speaker: Judge
content: Order! Court is now in session. Bring in the defendant, Aster Wynne!
The Origami Killer is dressed in ordinary clothes. Her face is pale and gaunt, bearing the sickly pallor one would find in patients with chronic illness.
She displays a perfect look of bewilderment, placing her right hand over her chest as she acknowledges the judge and jury.
She appears to be someone highly skilled at deception and exploiting the system. It's no wonder Forensica's investigation kept hitting dead ends.

speaker: Judge
content: Defendant Aster Wynne, how do you plead?

speaker: Aster
content: Your Honor, I cannot enter a plea. I was arrested without warning in my own home and brought to this court without even being informed of the charges against me.

speaker: Aster
content: Or is evidence and arrest warrants simply not required in DisCity? The citizens here can be arbitrarily detained, just like this?

speaker: Aster
content: I was expelled from the Forensic Association years ago. The little money I managed to scrape together from odd jobs barely covers my medical bills. Where would I possibly find the time or energy to commit crimes?
Aster coughs twice, perfectly timed. The jury members exchange uneasy glances and murmur among themselves. The judge's expression darkens.

This trial was rushed, and you were the one who forced it forward. Most details of the case remain unclear, which has drawn considerable criticism from the prosecution already. If you fail to uncover the truth here, your reputation will suffer as well.
Aster's eyes sweep across the courtroom before settling on you. For a brief moment, her expression shifts. It's subtle, yet she's unmistakably mocking you.

speaker: Judge
content: The prosecution may proceed.

Your Honor, members of the jury. We are not here today to discuss a simple murder case. We are here to expose a years-long, meticulously planned criminal conspiracy. The defendant, Aster Wynne, has used her expertise as a forensic pathologist to commit a series of perfect murders.

Ms. Wynne was expelled jointly by DisCity University's School of Forensic Science and the Forensic Association. The official reason cited was misconduct, but according to our investigation, the truth is that she lacks basic respect for human life and has repeatedly violated professional ethical standards.

speaker: Aster
content: This is slander against my character. I was expelled due to certain... misunderstandings at the time.

speaker: Aster
content: Furthermore, administrative sanctions cannot constitute direct evidence of murder. This is nothing but defamation.
I must ask you to refrain from interrupting. You will have ample opportunity to respond after I've finished presenting my case.
And given how much you'll need to refute, would you like me to provide you with paper so that you may take notes?
Then again, as a top graduate of DisCity University's School of Forensic Science, I'm sure you can manage without.
It seems you've picked up Forensica's habit of speaking without knowing it—your words are laced with sarcasm.
It certainly is satisfying though, being able to make someone squirm while you remain perfectly composed.
Aster seems to notice this as well. Her expression shifts briefly, and she glances around the room, carefully and subtly, as though searching for someone.
She presses her right hand to her chest, perhaps because she's struggling to withstand such verbal assault. Her expression takes on one of wounded grievance.

Shortly after your expulsion, the first Origami Killer case occurred. Since then, at regular intervals, cases with identical methods would arise—victims would seemingly die by suicide or accident, but every scene would be marked by a single origami flower.

options: Show case files and autopsy report

content: We noticed special paper fibers from the throat tissue samples of the most recent victim. Laboratory analysis confirms they're identical to fiber samples extracted from the throats of previous victims.
These fibers originate from specialized recording paper used exclusively by the School of Forensic Science.

speaker: Aster
content: Plenty of people have access to that paper. That includes students, instructors, and even janitors at the department.
But not everyone would know how to weaponize it for murder.
Your movements were discreet, I'll admit. But you still left a trail.

options: Show the investigation report on Aster Wynne

content: This is a report documenting your movements over the past few years, including everyone you've contacted and every location you've visited.
Cross-referencing this data with the times and locations of the Origami Killer's crimes yields an overlap rate of nearly one hundred percent.

speaker: Aster
content: Is screening big data what you call an "investigation" here? And I just happened to be the poor soul who got flagged as the killer?
We didn't need to screen anything to obtain this data. If anything, I don't understand why no one thought to cross-reference it until now.

speaker: Aster
content: With all due respect, as a former forensic pathologist, I wouldn't even classify this as evidence.

speaker: Aster
content: You're... the MBCC Chief, correct? Perhaps you should focus on what you actually do best instead.
A textbook deflection. I must be on the right track.
There's no need to rush. The key evidence will be submitted by another witness. I'm just here to present what I need to.
Based on the investigative findings, I charge the defendant with the following crimes—
First, the murder of at least seven victims. The modus operandi demonstrates a high degree of consistency with distinctive characteristics. This series of crimes has been classified as serial murder.

Second, following the commission of said murders, the defendant deliberately left origami flowers at each scene as both a provocation and a signature. Furthermore, utilizing their expert knowledge of forensic examination procedures and evidentiary protocols, the defendant systematically misdirected investigations by staging scenes to resemble suicides or accidental deaths, thereby obstructing justice, impeding investigation, and demonstrating contempt for the law.

Third, during the investigation of the Eligy case, the defendant exploited professional connections to illegally obtain private information about the victim's family. She then coerced the family members into withdrawing their report and refusing an autopsy, substantially perverting the course of justice and causing the case to remain misclassified for years.

As you finish speaking, the courtroom falls into a heavy silence. But even under the watchful eyes of the jury, as well as the forensic academy's faculty and students, Aster remains completely composed.
The killer possesses an iron will. Her expression remains unchanged. If anything, she seems to be wearing a faint, sardonic smile.
I request permission to call our witness.
The judge nods in approval. The side door opens, and Forensica's figure appears behind it.
Aster's smile freezes. But a moment later, a genuinely pleased expression crosses her face.
Unlike the mere curiosity of the others, she gazes at Forensica with an almost fanatical intensity.

speaker: Judge
content: Please state your identity for the record. You are Foren—

speaker: Forensica
content: Forensica. Former member of the Forensic Association... and a Sinner of the MBCC.
Forensica cuts off the judge and introduces herself. You didn't expect her to introduce herself like that, and you meet her eyes in surprise.
Does this mean that regardless of how the trial ends, she's willing to go under the supervision of the MBCC?

speaker: Forensica
content: Long time no see, senior.

speaker: Aster
content: I'm glad to hear you call me that. Of all my juniors, you were always the one I had the highest hopes for.

speaker: Forensica
content: And I'm equally glad to see you standing in the defendant's dock.
Forensica's gaze locks onto Aster. She doesn't blink, as if the slightest lapse in attention might allow Aster to slip away.

speaker: Forensica
content: The paper balls puzzled me for the longest time. I couldn't figure out what kind of killer would be so obsessed with them.

speaker: Forensica
content: A novelist who works with words? A courier who delivers documents? A factory worker who makes paper, or perhaps someone who recycles it?

speaker: Forensica
content: I was so fixated on the paper that I lost sight of the murders themselves.

speaker: Forensica
content: Being able to disguise the true cause of death using so many different methods—that in itself is a display of expertise.

speaker: Forensica
content: The person I was up against wasn't some cunning criminal. It was a forensic pathologist with the same level of expertise as mine.
Aster seems almost... pleased to see such a look from Forensica. She even smiles as she responds.

speaker: Aster
content: I appreciate the recognition, truly. But I can't confess to something I didn't do.

speaker: Aster
content: By that logic, any forensic pathologist could be a suspect.

speaker: Forensica
content: I went back to the school and examined all the forensic notes. Including yours.

speaker: Forensica
content: Your notes were exemplary. They've always been used as reference material.

speaker: Forensica
content: But there was something I noticed—some of the pages weren't quite flat. They looked like they'd been folded and smoothed out again, and they were stained with unidentified tissue fluid.

speaker: Forensica
content: Nearly every forensic pathologist is a perfectionist. They prefer clean, flat paper, and if their notes get stained during documentation, they're bound to make another copy.

speaker: Forensica
content: But you didn't do that. You left those creases and stains on the pages. That's because to you, they weren't imperfections. They were proof of your success.

speaker: Aster
content: Success? Perfectionist? My, I didn't expect you, out of all people, to stereotype our profession like that. And what exactly does this prove? That I'm a sloppy pathologist who doesn't mind a few wrinkles?

speaker: Forensica
content: Murdering someone through suffocation by paper ball—that couldn't have been perfected on the first try, could it?

speaker: Forensica
content: The size of the paper ball, the duration of suffocation, how to insert it precisely, and how to remove it completely intact...

speaker: Forensica
content: You must have spent a long time trying to perfect all of that. Those creases and stains are proof of this.

speaker: Forensica
content: Those seemingly random scribbles on the pages? They're the data from every "experiment" you've conducted.

speaker: Aster
content: All I hear are speculations. Where's your evidence?

speaker: Aster
content: Surely you don't intend to convict me based on nothing but subjective theories?

speaker: Forensica
content: Of course not. The evidence is on you.

speaker: Forensica
content: It's being kept in the pocket at your chest, to be precise.
The bailiffs exchange a glance before quickly restraining Aster's hands and retrieving a small notebook from said pocket.
The notebook reeks of disinfectant and formalin, but even that cannot mask the underlying stench of decay.
The gloved examiner opens the notebook. The pages inside are secured with ring fasteners and, just as Forensica said, bear jagged creases and stains.

speaker: Forensica
content: I kept wondering where those paper balls used in the murders ended up.

speaker: Forensica
content: If the killer wanted to commit the perfect crime, they would have destroyed the paper balls.

speaker: Forensica
content: But the killer was confident that the true cause of death would never be discovered. And so, these paper balls became more than just murder weapons—they became trophies. Medals of victory.

speaker: Forensica
content: That's why you kept them so close to your body. Isn't that right?
The stains on the notebook only need to be tested, and one will be able to see whether they match the victims' DNA.
The murder weapon, the method, and the movement patterns presented earlier—all of it forms an irrefutable chain of evidence.
Aster takes a deep breath. Her expression contorts, becoming a volatile mix of excitement, frustration, anger, and disappointment.

speaker: Aster
content: ...I didn't expect you to find me this fast.

speaker: Aster
content: It shouldn't have been like this...

speaker: Aster
content: You lost power, just like I did. You should've been scrambling through all the little traps I laid out, desperate, frantic. You should've been sneaking around for scraps of evidence still, catching glimpses of hope only to watch them slip away, over and over again.

speaker: Aster
content: And just when you'd start doubting yourself, I'd appear to reveal the truth—proclaiming to the world that I alone am the victor!

speaker: Aster
content: Or... you'd catch me making a mistake, take me prisoner, and then... you'd become the next me!

speaker: Forensica
content: That's impossible. I would never doubt myself.

speaker: Forensica
content: I'm the best forensic pathologist there is. The best.

speaker: Forensica
content: Period.
She'd never become someone like you, either.

speaker: Aster
content: Is that so? Hehe... But I've already achieved half of my goals... or it might be more accurate to say that I've already won.

speaker: Aster
content: You and I are the same. What you hate most are those meaningless rules, and all that social decorum.

speaker: Aster
content: You caught me, sure. So what?

speaker: Aster
content: Did you not utilize what you despise most to get here? Authority that oversteps its bounds, an institution that shields wrongdoing?

speaker: Aster
content: The dead can't be brought back to life. The institutional credibility you've put your faith in is worthless. What good is truth when it comes too late?

speaker: Aster
content: Did you think you'd be able to restore your status as a forensic pathologist? Or maybe you just wanted to savor the taste of victory?

speaker: Aster
content: My dear junior... you're just satisfying your own desires. You're just like me.
Forensica stands behind the witness stand, her lips pressed into a tight line, face drained of color. She offers no response.
I'll repeat myself again—she'd never become someone like you.
The rules, the authority, and the public trust you claim to despise... those are the very things you relied on.
Whether you realized it or not, when you conducted those experiments, indulging your desires and selfishness, you were relying on authority.

This world functions because of these things you hate so much. The difference is that some use these things to corrupt the world, while others wield them with conviction to pursue happiness and justice.
The judge strikes the gavel and delivers the verdict. Bailiffs escort Aster into custody, but this is not the end of the case. It is only the beginning.
The full extent of Aster's crimes has yet to be revealed. Many details still need to be uncovered, and some victims have yet to be found.

Outside the Courthouse, After the Trial

content: I... I came early to pack! You know that Ninety-Nine is too obvious. If I took her into the city, there would be a whole team after us in a second.

speaker: Hella
content: She doesn't have any common sense, it would be asking for trouble. And, she's pissed off a lot of people. You know better than I do!
Yeah, that's right.
So, now what? Now that I've caught you, are you going to resist arrest? Or are you going back to the Bureau with me?
Hella makes a noise.

speaker: Hella
content: Hmph! I, the great Hella, know when I've been beat!

speaker: Hella
content: I'll... go back to the Bureau with you...
Seeing that Hella has softened, you stand by the door and beckon to her.
Hella doesn't look at you, and runs back to pile all of her luggage into a trunk, then presses it to shut with her whole body weight.

speaker: Hella
content: Oh right! I forgot to stress this:

speaker: Hella
content: I am just staying there temporarily. Temporarily! Got it?

speaker: Hella
content: You better take good care of me, you hear? Or else I could just run away, like I did today!

speaker: Hella
content: That's right!

speaker: Hella
content: What question could you possibly still have?

speaker: Hella
content: If you've got something to say, then say it while I'm still in a good mood!
You straighten your uniform and clear your throat, then very properly ask Hella.
Since you have agreed to come with me to "stay temporarily," then, may I take that to mean... that we are friends now?
This time, Hella's face turns as red as a beet.
She lowers her head and quietly mumbles something.
What did you say? I couldn't hear you.
The girl raises her head and moves her lips, but no sound comes out.
Yeeees...?
You draw the word out.

speaker: Hella
content: I said...
Go on, I'm listening.
Hella can't take your teasing anymore, and yells out unhappily.

speaker: Hella
content: I said! Thank you! Thank you for saving us! Thank you for curing Ninety-Nine's infection!
When she's done, Hella picks up her suitcase and runs out without looking back.
She is... not even a little bit candid.
At that moment, you hear a knock on the door. You look back, and you see Nightingale looking coolly at you with arms crossed.

speaker: Nightingale
content: Chief, could you give me a reason that you and the target are in a building in the opposite direction of where you said she would be?
You curse under your breath and start thinking of an excuse.
Hrm... Maybe it's because, since I was still recovering from my fight with Ninety-Nine, I mixed up the directions for a moment.

speaker: Nightingale
content: "In order to evade capture, the target relocated. The Chief was concerned about a delay, and acted alone." I will put that in the formal report.
Thank you, Nightingale.
In the end, this farce of a prison break was resolved in just under half a day.
In the final submitted report, you record in detail the process of arresting the escapee Hella, uncovering her nest in the Syndicate southern district.
As for the loot and evidence, Nightingale and a group of officers packed it all up and carried it back to the Bureau.
